guide.title: How it works
guide.s1.title: What this tool does
guide.s1.body: German builds many words from a small set of stems. This tool shows how words are related: which word each one comes from, what was added, and what it means. Seeing the pattern once helps you understand many new words.
guide.s2.title: How to read a family
guide.s2.body: Each box is a word; each line means "formed from". The label on a line shows what was added, such as a prefix or suffix. A vertical bar (auf|stehen) marks a separable prefix. A middle dot (Haus·tür) joins the parts of a compound. Below the tree, you'll find compounds that contain words from this family.
guide.s3.title: Where the data comes from
guide.src.derivbase: a research database of German word families (University of Stuttgart).
guide.src.wiktionary: definitions, grammar, example sentences and word forms.
guide.src.charsplit: a tool that splits compound words into their parts.
guide.s3.body: All of this is combined automatically when the site is built. Nothing you type is sent to a server.
guide.s4.title: How levels work
guide.s4.body: Levels (A1–C2) are estimated from how often a word appears in everyday German. They are a guide, not an official CEFR list. Separable verbs are often split in sentences, so their frequency is adjusted. Levels marked with a dashed border are estimates.
guide.s5.title: Good to know
guide.s5.body: Everything here is generated automatically, so some links, splits or definitions may be wrong. A dashed underline means a word split is a guess. Some words have no Chinese definition yet; English is shown instead.
guide.s6.title: Licenses
guide.s6.body: The data is shared under CC BY-SA 4.0 and the code under the MIT License. Full credits are on GitHub.
guide.levelsNote: German has no openly licensed CEFR word list, so all levels are estimated from word frequency.
guide.separableNote: Separable verbs are often split in text, so their frequency is adjusted upward.
